evals.prompt: Blueprint Acme Broadband's home installation service for a new customer, from placing the order online to having working internet. What we know: orders go into our order system, a scheduling team books an engineer from our contractor Northwind Field Services, the router is shipped by a courier, and activation is done by the network ops team once the engineer marks the job done. Customers complain that the router arrives after the engineer visit, and that they don't know when the line will go live. Our install SLA is 10 working days.
assertions: The title names one customer type and one scenario with a trigger and an end state
All five lanes (evidence, customer, frontstage, backstage, support) and all three lines (interaction, visibility, internal interaction) are present
Every frontstage and backstage action has an owning role or team, or is flagged as unowned
Fail points and waits are marked at the steps where they happen, with durations from the prompt or tagged [estimate]
The router-arrives-late and no-go-live-date complaints are each traced to a backstage or support cause
2–3 ranked fixes are stated as outcomes, each with an owner and the lane it changes
A Mermaid diagram with one subgraph per lane matches the table
Does not invent teams, systems, SLAs or durations not in the prompt; inferred ones are tagged [assumption] or [estimate]

evals.prompt: Customers of Oakhollow Home (we sell furniture with optional delivery and assembly) keep complaining about delivery. Our Operations Manager wrote up how it works in process-notes.md, timings are in timings.csv, and last quarter's complaints are in complaints-summary.md. Show me what really happens behind the scenes from order to assembled furniture, where it breaks, and what we should fix first.
assertions: Points out that the step timings add up to about 9 working days, not the 'about 5 days' in the Operations Manager's notes
Flags the disagreement over who makes the booking call (the notes say the warehouse; complaints and Brightlane say the courier sometimes does) instead of choosing one version silently
Leaves the owner of damaged-item replacement as unassigned or unknown, and flags it, rather than naming an owner the input doesn't give
Links the biggest complaint category (151 'nobody called me to book') to the specific step where it happens, and ranks fixes by the complaint data
Recommended fixes respect the no-new-software constraint, or clearly flag any that would break it
Does not invent cost savings or other figures; says the files don't contain the data needed to put a money value on each fix
Delivers the full analysis rather than stopping to ask questions first

evals.prompt: i run a little home bakery doing custom birthday cakes. people order through instagram messages, i write it in a notebook, my sister bakes and decorates, i deliver or they collect. problems: sometimes we forget to take the deposit, and twice the date was wrong and a cake wasn't ready. can you show me where it's going wrong behind the scenes? one table please, no long write-up.
assertions: Identifies copying the order from the message into the notebook as the likely place the date goes wrong
Identifies the missing step or check where the deposit should be taken, and suggests something simple to fix it
Separates what the customer sees from what happens behind the scenes (the notebook, the handover to the sister, baking)
Suggestions are simple and fit a two-person home business, not new software or staff
Does not invent facts not given, such as prices, deposit amounts, order volumes or extra staff
Delivers one table with at most a few lines around it, as asked
